handbook.a1: Everything runs off the button in the top corner. It reads Continue on a quiet week and Matchday when you have a fixture. Press it and the world moves: the week advances, other results come in, and anything that happened lands in your inbox on the Home screen.
handbook.a10: A pre-match briefing that reads the opponent and suggests a full tactical setup, applied with one tap. A better assistant gives better advice. It is a starting point, not an instruction.
handbook.a11: The single loudest true thing about the match ahead - win and you go top, the board meets Monday regardless, a man is one try short of fifty, an old rival you have lost to three times running. It reads the table, the boardroom, the grudge book and the milestones the same way you could, and says out loud whichever one matters most this week. It says nothing when there is honestly nothing to say - a mid-table October Tuesday gets silence, not a manufactured headline.
handbook.a12: A great deal. Each referee has his own tolerance, and some will reach for a card where others talk. A yellow puts you a man down for ten minutes and the scoreboard usually shows it. A red is worse: the player leaves the field, and he picks up a ban of one or more matches afterwards. Aggressive players and the Hot Head trait get carded more.
handbook.a13: Yes, and it is a gamble rather than a free go. The panel reads the player's record: a player with a clean record on a one-match ban wins about two hearings in three, a repeat offender on a long ban almost never does, and most appeals fall somewhere near a coin toss. Win and a match comes off. Lose and a match goes on, and the board notes that you wasted everyone's afternoon.
handbook.a14: Rain and wind both make handling and kicking harder and push games towards the forwards. Snow more so. A wet afternoon is a good week to have picked a big pack and a boot.
handbook.a15: It plays the match out immediately and shows you the full-time score and report, without the tick-by-tick. Useful for a friendly or a week you do not want to sit through. You keep every consequence: injuries, cards, ratings and all.
handbook.a16: The dressing room asks you before kick-off. Full commentary is the match as it happens in commentary and live stats, with the pitch shown for tries and the big moments. Big moments runs the ticker straight to the next thing that matters, so you stop for scores, cards and injuries but not for every ruck, and half-time and the hour are still yours. Assistant hands the touchline to your assistant and takes you straight to the report. Your answer is remembered for that competition, so you can watch the league and skip the friendlies, and the cog during a match switches between the first two at any time.
handbook.a17: Five and three is the orthodox 23 and it is exactly neutral: cover everywhere, a weapon nowhere. Six and two is a bomb squad, and once three of your replacements are on it sharpens the scrum, the breakdown and the defence at the cost of attacking shape. Four and four is the reverse bargain: width and insurance, at the cost of the shove. Neither pays if you leave the bench sitting there.
handbook.a18: Cover. Name six forwards and you have two backs behind you, so a centre limping off after both have been used leaves a flanker finishing the game at 13. That costs you real attacking shape and leaks more in defence than it loses in attack, and no amount of shove up front makes it back. It is the price of the bomb squad, not a bug.
handbook.a19: Because players are people. Every man carries two things the game never shows you as a number: how consistent he is week to week, and what a big occasion does to him. A metronome turns up every Saturday; a mood player is capable of anything and its opposite; some grow an inch walking out for a final or a derby and some freeze. Favourites feel the weight too - on the big day the gap between the teams closes a touch, which is why cup upsets happen. None of it is on any screen: you learn who is who the way a real coach does, by watching a season of ratings. And during a match your assistant reports condition the same way - "blowing", "tiring", "out on his feet" - because nobody on a touchline knows a man is at exactly 43%.
handbook.a2: Three things, in order. You confirm the XV and the bench on the Tactics screen. You pick a dressing-room talk, and the words you choose move morale for real. Then you confirm you are ready, which is the last point at which you can change anything before the whistle.
handbook.a20: What you say to a replacement as he pulls his shirt on, set per bench seat on the Tactics bench page. Do the same job is neutral. Make an impact buys carrying at the cost of defence, and he tires quickly. Calm it down buys tackling and discipline and takes fewer risks in attack. Kill the clock kicks for territory to keep play in their half. Only the first three briefed players to come on take effect, so a bench is a decision rather than a stack of free upgrades.
handbook.a21: It is the ledger of what every player at the club has been told against what the team sheets actually say. Set his understanding (key player, rotation, squad player, prospect, or not in plans) and the page shows the appearances he was entitled to expect, what he has had, and how he feels about the gap. A player short of what he was promised gets restless and eventually wants out; telling him the truth costs nothing but the truth.
handbook.a22: Only for leaving out players you told otherwise, and only players who are not in the current matchday twenty-three. Nobody in this week's squad has a grievance this week. A frozen-out player settles at a grudge rather than sliding to total despair, so the consequence shows up as transfer requests, office visits and contract trouble rather than as a hidden penalty on the side you field.
handbook.a23: Four portfolios beyond the armband: who leads the pack, who calls the defensive line, who runs the attack, and who sets the standards. A portfolio does not make the side stronger. It concentrates the leadership you already have onto one area and takes it off the rest, so naming a defensive leader sharpens the defence at the cost of attacking shape. Only starters with real authority can carry one, and a real leader can carry more than one: each portfolio is its own trade, so a second job concentrates more of the side onto his areas rather than stacking a bonus.
handbook.a24: Attributes are shown on a 1 to 100 scale and describe what he can do. Current Ability is a single 1 to 100 summary of how good he is now, Potential is how good he could become, and Potential stays hidden until your scouting knowledge of him is good enough. Form is a rolling 1 to 10 on recent performances, morale is how he feels, condition is how fresh he is, and sharpness is how much rugby he has played lately.
handbook.a24_f: Attributes are shown on a 1 to 100 scale and describe what she can do. Current Ability is a single 1 to 100 summary of how good she is now, Potential is how good she could become, and Potential stays hidden until your scouting knowledge of her is good enough. Form is a rolling 1 to 10 on recent performances, morale is how she feels, condition is how fresh she is, and sharpness is how much rugby she has played lately.
handbook.a25: Tap Team and you land on the team sheet. Best XV asks your assistant for his best side - a strong draft that quietly weighs form, but it is his eye, not an answer key. Adjust by hand - tap a player, tap another, and they swap - and the corrections are yours. Tap the same slot twice for the full squad picker. How the side plays (roles, set piece, bench shape, prep, game plan) lives on the Tactics screen.
handbook.a26: Your assistant names the side, and it stays named: nobody updates an untouched sheet for form, fitness or new signings, and the assistant is decent, not perfect - he misjudges a man here and there, less often the higher his level. Picking the XV yourself is always worth real points over a season, and so is upgrading the assistant if you want to delegate. The press desk works the same way: questions left to rot cost a little board confidence and fan mood every time, so silence is a choice with a price.
handbook.a27: On the Tactics tab each shirt can be given a role that shapes how he plays: a ball-playing ten, a fetcher at seven, a sweeping full back. A role suits some players more than others, and it works best on a man whose attributes already point that way.
handbook.a28: Five pairings build familiarity by playing together: the two props either side of the hooker, the lock pairing, the halfbacks, and the centres. A settled pairing goes from brand new to settling in, settled, established and eventually telepathic, and each step is worth something real. Rotating those five slots every week costs you more than it looks.
handbook.a29: Pair any player aged 20 or under who is still below his potential with a senior pro of 28 or more, on the Mentoring tab of the Team Report. Four pairings at a time, five with a Centre of Excellence at level 3 or better. Choose the young player first and every senior who could take him is listed with how close their positions are, his leadership, his caps and what he could teach. Nobody knows how the two will get on until they try: for the first month the card only says it is too early to tell, and after that it says in plain words how it is going. Character decides most of it: a Leader teaching an Ambitious or Temperamental kid is the best combination in the game, two Temperamentals together the worst, and a Mercenary teaches almost nothing. The same position helps, the same unit (front row, back five, halves, outside backs) a little, and experience a little more. Each week the pairing can coach a point into something the senior is clearly better at and the kid's position needs, paid for from the kid's least needed attributes like all training, and can add a rating point while he is below his potential: about one a season for an average pairing. A senior can take two kids, but each then learns at three-quarter speed, and he will mention it in the eight-week reports. Slowly the kid may also take on his mentor's character, roughly a one in three chance across a season. The Mentoring tab keeps a record of what each kid has gained. A pairing ends itself when there is nothing left to teach (the kid turns 21, reaches his ceiling or takes on his mentor's character), and one that is not working can be ended on its card.
handbook.a3: Yes, at any stoppage. The clipboard button opens tactics and substitutions mid-match, so you can shut a game down, chase one, or get a tiring front row off. Eight men sit on the bench and you can use all eight, which is what the laws allow: front-row cover included. A man who has come off does not come back, other than the front-row and blood exceptions the referee panel already applies. The game suggests natural cover first rather than putting a winger in the second row.
handbook.a30: Three layers. The whole squad has a weekly emphasis; up to five youngsters can carry a development focus for faster growth; and a handful of men can be put on personal plans, individual programmes in a chosen area. Your assistant's badge sets how many plans the department can run at once, the matching specialist coach and the Training Paddock make a plan bite more often, and younger men absorb more of it. A man on a plan works his programme instead of the squad session, so it is a choice, not a stack. Progress is slow and unglamorous, which is how it should be. Training decides where ability goes, not how much there is: every point a programme adds is paid for by a point from an area it does not cover, taken from what the position needs least, and it stops near what the position plays at. A plan also adds one rating point each summer to anyone below their potential.
handbook.a31: Your backroom staff are named people, each holding an Unbadged, Bronze, Silver or Gold badge. The badge is what they are worth to you. You can send a coach on a course to try for the next one: sixty thousand pounds per tier, and about 58 in every 100 pass. The examiners decide the same day, so you know before the weekend. The fee is spent either way, and a coach who fails cannot sit it again for four weeks.
handbook.a32: Watch condition and minutes. A player who passes 1,300 minutes in a season is in the red zone and starts breaking down. Rotate, use the recovery preparation on short turnarounds, and build the gym: each level of the Strength and Conditioning Gym buys back condition every single week.
handbook.a33: A better physio and a better Recovery Centre both shorten layoffs. The Medical Centre screen lists everyone out, with return dates. You can pay for a specialist consult on a bad one, and wrap a man with a long injury record in cotton wool for a week. Head injuries follow the HIA protocol and the length of the layoff is not yours to decide.
handbook.a34: A signature edge, or flaw. The Step beats defenders and scores tries, Siege Gun kicks from anywhere, Jackal wins turnovers, Big-Game Player grows in knockouts and derbies, Hot Head is one flashpoint from a card every week. They show on the player's profile and they change what happens on the field.
handbook.a35: Leadership is the attribute that matters, and the Leadership card on the Team screen's Selection tab lists your squad sorted by it. A strong captain lifts attack and defence and keeps tempers in check. Name a vice-captain too: he steps up at half the effect when the skipper is missing, and one day he will take the armband for good.
handbook.a36: In week 2 of every season the office asks how you want to pitch the year against the pundits' predicted finish, and your answer stands until the summer. Aim high and every result is measured against your own words: wins earn about 15 per cent more boardroom credit, defeats cost about 30 per cent more - the pressure is the price of the promise. Keep heads down and the boardroom needle is muted 15 per cent in both directions: safer when losing, thinner credit when winning. Back the board's targets and results are judged the way they always were. There is no secretly correct answer - it is a bet on your own season.
handbook.a37: The forced page between seasons. When the final whistle of a campaign has gone and the summer has been processed, Continue lands on the Annual: the year's champions, your silverware if there was any, and confirmation that the season is filed - the Roll of Honour, your Annals on the Manager Legacy screen and the record books are all written up before you see it. One button starts the new season, and nothing advances until you press it.
handbook.a38: The ambition you chose for this career, at the foot of the New Career wizard - take a Championship club into the top flight, win the league and Europe with one club, build a first team out of your own academy, coach a nation to the World Championship, and a handful more. It is offered fresh from your starting club, so a Premier Division giant is never asked to "reach the top flight" and an English National One side is never asked to "win it all with what you have got." It sits on the Home screen every week with an honest line on where it stands, gets a verdict in every season review, and is graded on the Manager Legacy screen at the end of the career. It changes nothing about how a match plays out - it is a lens on the save, not a lever in it.
handbook.a39: A youth intake arrives every season. Your academy coach and the Centre of Excellence both raise the quality of what comes through, and the better your setup the more likely a genuine prospect appears. You get an honest preview before intake day and a graded report afterwards. Development deals run out at 21: promote a lad to a professional contract from his player page before the summer he turns 21, or he leaves as a free agent. You are warned a full season ahead.
handbook.a4: The Game Plan tab splits into two halves: With the Ball is the four attacking sliders, Without the Ball is how the fifteen defend. Line Speed trades defensive muscle for discipline - a blitz makes more tackles and more turnovers but gives away more penalties and cards, a drift stays clean and gives them room. Width is a matchup call read at kick-off: a wide defensive line smothers an expansive attack but a tight pick-and-go side runs through the middle of it, and a narrow line does the reverse. Both dials start at the balanced midpoint, where they cost and buy nothing. Every other dugout sets them too - a Blitz Defence coach flies off the line, a Counter-Punch side soaks - and the briefing card names the opponent's defensive shape so your attack can answer it.
handbook.a40: Yes, but only when something weakens its hand, and the player page tells you what that is before you bid. The strongest card you can hold is a contract running out in the summer, because they would otherwise lose him for nothing. After that: a man who has barely played, one who is unhappy, a club sitting in the red, a squad already well stocked in his position, or a player the wrong side of 33. Those stack, up to about a third off in the worst case for the seller. A wanted man who is playing every week at a solvent club will not move a penny, and the screen says so rather than letting you waste a window finding out.
handbook.a41: Two stages. First the fee: the stepper starts at the asking price and you move up or down from there, and a low bid can be refused outright. Then personal terms: weekly wage, a signing-on fee, and perks. His camp will accept, counter or walk. A promise of first-team rugby softens the wage he will take, and it is a real promise that gets remembered.
handbook.a42: Your wage budget is a weekly ceiling on what the squad can cost. Two players can be named marquee, and their wages sit outside that ceiling, which is how you keep one star you could not otherwise afford. Everyone else counts.
handbook.a43: Three ways. Set a focus league and your scout builds knowledge there over time. Watch the Scouting Agency boards for players the world is talking about. Or commission a specific search from the Shortlist tab: a three, six or nine-month brief for a named position. The longer the brief and the better the scout, the better the name that comes back, and the written report grades what the scout found.
handbook.a44: Because you do not know him yet. Scouting knowledge runs 0 to 100 and rises as your scouts watch him. Below a certain point his potential is a range, not a number. Your own players are fully known from day one.
handbook.a45: A player in the final season of his deal can be signed on a free to join you next summer. He sees the season out at his club, who find out from the press release. It is the cheapest way to improve a squad and everyone else is doing it too.
handbook.a46: Two, and the game tells you when one is closing. Deadline week is flagged on the Home screen, bids start lapsing, and panic bargains appear late on. The Deals tab on the Transfer Centre is one screen for everything you have in flight.
handbook.a47: A player who is performing above his contract will have his camp come knocking. You can meet the demand, haggle a figure of your own, or refuse. Refusing a star has consequences, and so does paying every time.
handbook.a48: Yes, and you should for young players who are not going to get minutes. A postcard arrives from the feeder club telling you how he is doing. Loans in belong to your current project: take a new job and they go home. Loans have gravity, too: a player will step down one division for game time, but two is rare - a National League club borrows from the Championship, and only the odd hungry youngster drops all the way from a top flight.
handbook.a49: Yes. On his profile, The Office card lets you praise his form or have a quiet word - two conversations a week across the squad, one per man. His personality decides how it lands: a professional answers a warning with work, a mercenary shrugs, and praising a struggling hothead reads as sarcasm. Warning a man who is playing well insults him, and the dressing room hears about it.
handbook.a5: Yes, and Physicality is the dial he decides. Pushing it up buys breakdown power and costs you yellow cards and kickable penalties, and the penalty price scales with the man in the middle. Measured over eight seasons: in front of a referee who lets a lot go at the tackle, going physical is worth about two and a half points a match to you; in front of one who is fussy there, it costs you about a point and a half. Getting that read right is worth roughly four points a match, which is more than any other single slider is worth on its own. The referee and his interpretations are named on the pre-match briefing before you pick, so the information is always there. Left in the middle the dial costs and buys nothing.
handbook.a50: Twice a season, at the top of each window, the scouting department puts up to three names on the board - aimed at your thinnest positions and ageing shirts, every one inside your budget and wage room. The names come from your scouts' own view of the market, so a better-run department proposes better players. Tap a name in the memo to open his profile and bid.
handbook.a51: A 0 to 100 reading of how safe your job is. Results move it most, then the objectives you were set, then how you handle the press and whether you keep your promises. It appears on the Home dashboard, and a half-term report card spells out where you stand. Let it fall far enough and you will be sacked. The board's patience scales with who you manage: a genuine title favourite has a thin-skinned board that reacts hard to every swing, so a season adrift of the trophy is a real crisis - stay hands-off there and you can be out of a job by the spring. A club with modest ambitions has a patient one that barely reacts to a mid-table finish, because nobody expected more. Same numbers, same rules, a very different ride depending on the crest on your shirt.
handbook.a52: In: a weekly commercial and broadcast share set by the club's reputation, gate receipts from home matches, club shop takings, prize money at the end of the season, and transfer fees. Out: player wages, backroom wages, upkeep on the ground and the estate, and whatever you spend. The Finances screen lists every line.
handbook.a53: What it costs to open the doors, every week of the year, match or no match. The ground has to be heated, mown, stewarded and insured, and every facility level is a building with staff inside it. It is why upgrading is a commitment rather than a free ratchet: a better gym is a bill that keeps arriving. The figure is on the Finances screen.
handbook.a54: There are nine facilities and each runs from level 0 to level 5. You cannot buy them: you ask the board, on the Club Infrastructure page, and the board weighs the price against the reserves and its confidence in you. Confidence buys backing too: a board that rates you in the high seventies underwrites seventy per cent of the bill, seventy or better more than half, one just warming to you about a third, one that merely tolerates you nothing at all, and below forty-five the answer is no whatever the balance says. Approved work takes three weeks at the first level and twelve at the last, and a new stand takes twelve. Only one project runs at a time, and a refusal puts you on a two-month cooling-off period before you can ask again.
handbook.a55: Training Pitch: a true surface sharpens the breakdown and the handling in every match, and the squad develops faster on it; a bog blunts both and hurts people in training. Gym: condition recovered every week. Recovery Centre: shorter layoffs. Training Paddock: attribute training bites more often. Kicking Enclosure: sharper goal kicking. Briefing Suite: match preparation and the analyst both land harder. Centre of Excellence: better academy intakes. Club Shop: retail income every week, more when the fans are happy. Hospitality and Boxes: every home gate is worth 4 per cent more per level. Each card on the Infrastructure page states its current effect in plain numbers.
handbook.a56: Usually one of three reasons, and it says which. Not enough of the season played to judge demand, a ground that is not full enough as it is, or reserves that will not carry the build. There is a fourth: every club has a catchment, and once the ground holds about everyone who would come, more seats would be empty seats. The Infrastructure page states your catchment so you can see where the ceiling is.
handbook.a57: It did not take it, it spent it. A board will not let a large surplus sit in a deposit account while the club stands still, so over the summer anything well beyond a season of wages plus a float goes back into the club: a build on the estate, the ground debt, the academy, the community programme. The news item says what it went on, and the terraces notice.
handbook.a58: Yes. Fan mood runs from mutinous to bouncing and shows on the Home dashboard. A happy crowd turns up in bigger numbers, lifts the side at home, and buys more in the shop. Results move it, and so do signings, sales and the things you say in press conferences.
handbook.a59: Derbies are fixed by geography and history. Grudges you earn: a bad-tempered match, a poached player, a public dig. Both make the next meeting spicier, with more cards, a hostile crowd and a form book that means nothing. The club screen keeps the ledger.
handbook.a6: No, and it used to be. Winding Kicking up gives your kicking unit more of the game and pins them in their half, which is exactly what you want in wind and rain. It also means you carry less: your attack and your breakdown both drop for it. Across a season the two roughly cancel, so it is a read on the weather, the opposition and your own boot rather than a setting to leave at one end. If you have a siege gun at ten and a shaky pack, kick. If your strength is width and offloads, do not.
handbook.a60: Questions arrive before and after matches and you choose the tone of your answer. Confidence lifts your squad and needles the opposition, who will remember it. Caution keeps everyone calm. Promises made here are recorded, and broken ones cost you.
handbook.a61: New owners can arrive at your club. It usually means a war chest and a honeymoon period, and it always means new expectations. Sometimes it means neither and you have simply been sold to someone with less money.
handbook.a62: You have three things to sell: the front of the shirt, the naming rights to the ground, and the kit supply. Each is a contract with a value and a length, and the Commercial tab on the Finances screen is where you sign them. A long deal pays under the going rate because the sponsor is buying certainty off you. A short one pays over the odds and puts you back in the market sooner, which is where a good season is worth real money. Some offers carry a performance clause and start below market: deliver it and it is the best deal in the building, miss it and you have sold cheap.
handbook.a63: Deals run out. When one does you are told, and until you sign somebody that slot pays nothing at all, which is a real hole in a weekly budget. The three you inherit are staggered so they do not all fall due in the same summer, but they do fall due.
handbook.a64: Boxes and lounges make every home crowd worth more at the gate, four per cent per level. They also cost more to run than any other building on the estate, because a box needs chefs and hosts whether or not there is a match. Break-even is an average home crowd of about nine thousand across a season of roughly fourteen home gates, so at a full Premier Division ground a level returns about one and a half times its upkeep, and more again at a big one. Below that it is a straight loss. Expanding the ground adds seats; this makes the seats you have worth more.
handbook.a65: Every six weeks the league looks at what every club actually did across that window, counting league, cup and European matches alike. To be in the running at all a manager needs three matches and two wins from them, so a single good afternoon wins nothing. Beyond the bar it is merit: beating a better side counts for more than beating a worse one, winning away counts for more than winning at home, and the size of the win matters. If nobody in the league did enough, the award is not given that month.
handbook.a66: Build a reputation, then apply from the Job Centre when a vacancy that suits you appears. Your chances depend on your reputation against the club's standing. If you are doing well somewhere, bigger clubs will come to you: a tap on the shoulder arrives in your inbox, and it does not stay open long. And if you are out of work, modest clubs will give a second chance: experience in the dugout counts for more the further down you look, so the way back in is usually a rung or two below the job you left.
handbook.a67: It does. A public loyalty vow is recorded, and if you walk out within a few weeks of making one, every paper runs the clip. Your new board notes how cheaply the last promise was sold, and the away end has a song ready for your return.
handbook.a68: Your name, your record, your trophies and your badges. Not much else. The facilities belong to the club, so you inherit whatever the new one has. The backroom staff there are the backroom staff there. Grudges, the head-to-head book, the decisions ledger and the ground record all start blank, because they belong to the old place.
handbook.a69: A running list on your Profile of the choices that mattered: appointments, board requests, briefs, analyst reads you followed, expansions. Each is marked as having worked out or not. It is there so a long career has a story you can read back rather than a number.
handbook.a7: You do. When your side wins a penalty in range, the game stops and asks: posts, corner, or tap and go. Your kicker's goal kicking and the angle both matter, and so does the scoreboard. Taking three when you need seven is how games get lost.
handbook.a70: Because the room outranks you. The game compares your reputation to the standing of the 23 you pick: walk into a star dressing room as an unproven name and the squad re-examines every instruction - patterns drill at up to half pace, team talks land at a fraction of their weight, and a fine handed out by a manager without a record can blow up into a stand-off. The Manager Profile shows the standing line. The way out is the same as real life: deliver. Trust earned through results cancels the strain outright - a room that fully believes in you stops caring what your CV says - and a trophy ends the conversation for good.
handbook.a71: Yes, if one asks. The unions watch managers with a reputation of 64 or better and ring twice a season - the smaller nations first, England, France and New Zealand only for names in the mid-80s. Accept from your Manager Profile and you hold the country alongside the club: the Club & Country screen holds the whole desk - the ranking, the union's confidence, your Test record, and the window squad, which is yours to shape. When camp is open you can drop a name and call the next man up - any qualified player in the game, no age limit and no rating floor, only the injured refused - the federation caps the room and will not let it fall below 23, and on a Test weekend your assistant minds any club fixture while you take the country. Leave the job and the Test record stays on your Manager Profile for good. Step down from either job from the same screen. A World Championship is the biggest thing in the game. The Job Centre shows how close your reputation is.
handbook.a72: Every four years - 2027, 2031 and on. Twenty nations in four pools of five, seeded from the live world rankings so four years of Test results decide who lands the kind pool and who gets the group of death, then quarter-finals, semis and a final. It runs in the opening weeks of the season and your internationals are away with their countries until it is decided, so plan the early club rounds around the gaps. There is no Southern Championship and no autumn series that year: the World Championship is the Test calendar. Hold a national job when one comes around and you coach every match of it - your seeding sets the bar, the union marks you against it, and the post-mortem lands either way. A World Championship won stays on a player's honours for good, and on yours.
handbook.a73: In England the trapdoor is a game: the Premier Division's bottom club hosts the Championship winner in a one-off playoff after the finals, and the winner plays top-flight rugby next season. Everywhere else the swap is automatic - bottom of the top flight down, champion of the second tier up. European places come from final league standings: the top five of the Premier Division, six of the Elite 14 and five of the UPC make the Continental Cup, and the band below each of them goes into the Continental Shield.
handbook.a74: Three places. Manager Profile has your badges, specialities and trophy cabinet. Manager Legacy has the milestones. The Annals hold every season you have managed, one row each, and the Roll of Honour holds the world's: champions, Players of the Year, and the Hall of Fame.
handbook.a75: The game saves itself every week, so you cannot lose a season to a closed tab. Game Status has four slots for manual backups or parallel careers, a Send a copy button that hands the save to your phone's share sheet, and an Export Career button that writes it to a file. It all lives in this browser's storage, which is why those two matter: clearing your browsing data takes the career with it, and on an iPhone Safari clears the storage of sites it has not seen for a week or so unless the game is on your home screen.
handbook.a76: The dark theme, toggled by the button next to Continue. It is meant for reading a phone at night and everything in the game is built to work in it.
handbook.a77: Six: English, French, Spanish, Italian, Japanese and Afrikaans, chosen on the title screen directly below the text size - and answerable before a career exists, so you never have to start one in the wrong language to find the switch. It changes everything the game says to you, including the assistant's game plan, the coach's verdict and the analyst's read, which are written fresh every time you look at them. The match commentary and the stories in your inbox stay in the language they were written in: they are filed into the career as they happen, and a report that changed its words between two readings would not be a record of anything.
handbook.a78: Two ways, on the Save / Load screen. Send a copy hands the save file to your phone's own share sheet, so it goes to a cloud drive, a chat with yourself or an e-mail in two taps - that is the one that matters, because a file in Downloads is on the same phone as the career it is backing up. Export Career writes the file to the device instead, which is what a computer wants. Either file goes back in through Import on any device, and the game reminds you once a season because storage that clears itself is the only way this game can lose a career.
handbook.a79: It collects nothing. No account, no sign-in, no analytics, no advertising identifier - the game makes no network request at all once it has loaded, and the build fails automatically if anybody ever adds one. Everything is on your device. Where the game is sold through an app store it may offer one optional Supporter purchase, which puts a mark on the title screen: it buys no players, no budget and no result, because a management game where the paying manager wins more is a different game.
handbook.catWordsSub: the terms the game uses, in plain English
handbook.a80: The ball has gone out of play, so it is thrown back in down a corridor of forwards who lift a jumper to catch it. Win your own throw and you keep possession; steal theirs and you have the ball deep in their half.
handbook.a81: Eight forwards from each side bind together and push for a ball fed into the middle. It restarts play after a minor mistake, and a dominant pack wins penalties from it as well as possession.
handbook.a82: A tackled player puts the ball down and players from both sides bind over it, on their feet, trying to win it back. Nobody may use hands once it forms, which is why the fight for it is with feet and shoulders.
handbook.a83: The same contest as a ruck, but the ball carrier is still on his feet and players bind on to him. A strong pack drives it forward, which is how a lot of tries are scored from close range.
handbook.a84: The few seconds after a tackle, when possession is genuinely up for grabs. Most matches are decided here rather than in open field, which is why breakdown work is one of the things your forwards are rated on.
handbook.a85: A player who gets over a tackled opponent and grabs the ball before a ruck forms. Do it legally and you win a penalty; get it fractionally wrong and you give one away, which is why jackals are prized and risky.
handbook.a86: Possession changing hands during play rather than at a set piece. Turnovers are the cheapest tries in rugby, because the defence is usually out of position the moment one happens.
handbook.a87: Dropping the ball forwards. Play stops and the other side gets the scrum, which is why handling under pressure matters more than raw pace.
handbook.a88: A pass made in the tackle, before going to ground. It keeps the move alive and skips the ruck entirely - the fastest way through a set defence, and the easiest way to lose the ball.
handbook.a89: A try is five points and earns a conversion kick worth two more. A penalty kick at goal is three. A drop goal - kicked out of hand while play is live - is also three.
handbook.a90: The line twenty-two metres out from each try line. It matters for kicking: inside your own 22 you may kick straight into touch and keep the ground you gained, outside it you may not.
handbook.q91: Why kick to the corner instead of at the posts?
handbook.a91: Three points from the tee are near certain; the corner gives you a lineout five metres out and a chance at seven. Take the points when three is enough, take the corner when it is not.
handbook.a92: A short, high kick from the scrum-half, usually out of a ruck, meant to be chased and contested in the air. It is how a side escapes its own half without handing over easy possession.
handbook.q93: What is an up-and-under, or a grubber?
handbook.a93: An up-and-under is a high kick that hangs long enough for chasers to arrive under it. A grubber is kicked along the ground through a defence, for a chaser to gather behind them.
handbook.a94: Kick from inside your own half and put it into touch inside their 22, and you throw into the lineout instead of them. It rewards an accurate kick and drags defenders back to cover the space behind.
handbook.a95: A scrum or a lineout: play restarting from a fixed, organised position rather than a scramble. A side with a reliable set piece controls when the game speeds up, which is what your tight five are paid for.
handbook.q96: What is the gain line, and what is a phase?
handbook.a96: The gain line is the imaginary line across the pitch where the last ruck was - crossing it means you actually moved forward. A phase is one carry and the ruck that follows it, so 'six phases' means six carries with no whistle.
handbook.q97: Who are the front row, the tight five and the back row?
handbook.a97: The front row is two props and a hooker, the men who meet first in a scrum. Add the two locks and it is the tight five, the pushing engine. The back row - two flankers and a number 8 - are the forwards who cover ground.
handbook.q98: What do the scrum-half and fly-half do?
handbook.a98: The scrum-half feeds the ball out of every ruck and scrum, so he touches it more than anyone on the pitch. The fly-half decides what happens next - pass, kick or run - and is usually the goal kicker as well.
handbook.a99: The two wings and the full-back: the last line of defence and usually the quickest men in the side. They field kicks, chase them, and finish most of the tries.
handbook.q100: What is a 'bomb squad', or a 6-2 split?
handbook.a100: How you divide the eight replacements. A 6-2 split is six forwards and two backs, so you can change your whole pack late and out-muscle a tiring team. It leaves you thin if a back gets injured.
handbook.a101: The Television Match Official, who reviews a score or a piece of foul play on replay. In this game a TMO check means the outcome of a moment is not settled until the review comes back. Here the TMO can also rule a try out: about one try in six goes upstairs, and roughly a third of those are chalked off. A try with a forward pass in the build-up always goes to the TMO: nine in ten are ruled out, and the rest stand as tight calls.
handbook.q102: What are yellow and red cards, and the sin bin?
handbook.a102: A yellow card sends a player to the sin bin for ten minutes and you play a man short. A red card removes him for the rest of the match. Both cost far more than the penalty that caused them.
handbook.a104: A short-term signing to cover a long injury. When a player is out for six weeks or more, the Medical Centre lets you sign one free agent who plays that position. The wage sits outside the salary cap while the cover lasts, though the club still pays it every week, and the deal ends when the injured player is fit, leaves the club, or the season ends. One joker per injured player.
handbook.q105: Can an injured player play through it?
handbook.a105: In the last three weeks of a layoff, yes, from the Medical Centre. The injury becomes a knock: available to pick, but starting each match short of full energy, and every match played on it risks a flare-up and a longer layoff. The button states the risk: 20% a match sent back a week early, 46% three weeks early. Rest instead puts the layoff back as it was. A head injury is never played through.
handbook.q106: Does a big crowd sway the referee?
handbook.a106: On a big day it can. In front of a large home crowd, in a derby or in a knockout, the tight calls lean toward the home side, and the pre-match briefing says so when they will. It is the crowd, not the referee: the same match in front of empty stands would not lean.
handbook.q107: When does the pitch come on during a match?
handbook.a107: For the moments that matter. In between, the match is the commentary with the live stats underneath. Highlights in Match Settings (the cog on the match screen) chooses which moments: Key shows tries and tries sent to the TMO; Extended adds kicks at goal and breaks into the 22. A highlight plays the phases that led to it, then the finish, and the commentary keeps pace with the picture. In the last ten minutes of a close match (seven points or fewer in it), Key shows the kicks and the attacks too.
handbook.q108: Is a match I watch different from one I skip or play with Instant Result?
handbook.a108: No. Every match in the game, yours or anybody else's, watched line by line, skipped or played with Instant Result, runs on the same engine with the same rules. Watching only decides what is written down for you to read. When the other dugout changes its plan to counter you, the commentary says so.
handbook.a103: A Head Injury Assessment. A player who takes a blow to the head leaves the field to be checked; he returns only if he passes, and the game will not let him back if he does not.
handbook.a8: The week's training focus, set on the Tactics screen before the game. Attack, defence, set piece, fitness or recovery. It gives a small edge in that area for the coming match, and the Analysis and Briefing Suite makes the edge bigger. Recovery buys back condition instead, which is what you want on a short turnaround.
handbook.a9: Before each match he names the unit he thinks the opposition is weakest in. If he is right you get a small edge there, and you can turn his read straight into that week's preparation with one tap. He is not always right. His accuracy climbs with the Briefing Suite and with a better assistant, and the Prep page keeps his record so you can decide how much to trust him.

handbook.a11_f: The single loudest true thing about the match ahead - win and you go top, the board meets Monday regardless, a woman is one try short of fifty, an old rival you have lost to three times running. It reads the table, the boardroom, the grudge book and the milestones the same way you could, and says out loud whichever one matters most this week. It says nothing when there is honestly nothing to say - a mid-table October Tuesday gets silence, not a manufactured headline.
handbook.a12_f: A great deal. Each referee has his own tolerance, and some will reach for a card where others talk. A yellow puts you a woman down for ten minutes and the scoreboard usually shows it. A red is worse: the player leaves the field, and she picks up a ban of one or more matches afterwards. Aggressive players and the Hot Head trait get carded more.
handbook.a19_f: Because players are people. Every woman carries two things the game never shows you as a number: how consistent she is week to week, and what a big occasion does to her. A metronome turns up every Saturday; a mood player is capable of anything and its opposite; some grow an inch walking out for a final or a derby and some freeze. Favourites feel the weight too - on the big day the gap between the teams closes a touch, which is why cup upsets happen. None of it is on any screen: you learn who is who the way a real coach does, by watching a season of ratings. And during a match your assistant reports condition the same way - "blowing", "tiring", "out on her feet" - because nobody on a touchline knows a woman is at exactly 43%.
handbook.a20_f: What you say to a replacement as she pulls her shirt on, set per bench seat on the Tactics bench page. Do the same job is neutral. Make an impact buys carrying at the cost of defence, and she tires quickly. Calm it down buys tackling and discipline and takes fewer risks in attack. Kill the clock kicks for territory to keep play in their half. Only the first three briefed players to come on take effect, so a bench is a decision rather than a stack of free upgrades.
handbook.a21_f: It is the ledger of what every player at the club has been told against what the team sheets actually say. Set her understanding (key player, rotation, squad player, prospect, or not in plans) and the page shows the appearances she was entitled to expect, what she has had, and how she feels about the gap. A player short of what she was promised gets restless and eventually wants out; telling her the truth costs nothing but the truth.
handbook.a22_f: Only for leaving out players you told otherwise, and only players who are not in the current matchday twenty-three. Nobody in this week's squad has a grievance this week. A frozen-out player settles at a grudge rather than sliding to total despair, so the consequence shows up as transfer requests, office visits and contract trouble rather than as a hidden penalty on the side you field.
handbook.a23_f: Four portfolios beyond the armband: who leads the pack, who calls the defensive line, who runs the attack, and who sets the standards. A portfolio does not make the side stronger. It concentrates the leadership you already have onto one area and takes it off the rest, so naming a defensive leader sharpens the defence at the cost of attacking shape. Only starters with real authority can carry one, and a real leader can carry more than one: each portfolio is its own trade, so a second job concentrates more of the side onto her areas rather than stacking a bonus.
handbook.a26_f: Your assistant names the side, and it stays named: nobody updates an untouched sheet for form, fitness or new signings, and the assistant is decent, not perfect - he misjudges a woman here and there, less often the higher his level. Picking the XV yourself is always worth real points over a season, and so is upgrading the assistant if you want to delegate. The press desk works the same way: questions left to rot cost a little board confidence and fan mood every time, so silence is a choice with a price.
handbook.a27_f: On the Tactics tab each shirt can be given a role that shapes how she plays: a ball-playing ten, a fetcher at seven, a sweeping full back. A role suits some players more than others, and it works best on a woman whose attributes already point that way.
handbook.a29_f: Pair any player aged 20 or under who is still below her potential with a senior pro of 28 or more, on the Mentoring tab of the Team Report. Four pairings at a time, five with a Centre of Excellence at level 3 or better. Choose the young player first and every senior who could take her is listed with how close their positions are, her leadership, her caps and what she could teach. Nobody knows how the two will get on until they try: for the first month the card only says it is too early to tell, and after that it says in plain words how it is going. Character decides most of it: a Leader teaching an Ambitious or Temperamental kid is the best combination in the game, two Temperamentals together the worst, and a Mercenary teaches almost nothing. The same position helps, the same unit (front row, back five, halves, outside backs) a little, and experience a little more. Each week the pairing can coach a point into something the senior is clearly better at and the kid's position needs, paid for from the kid's least needed attributes like all training, and can add a rating point while she is below her potential: about one a season for an average pairing. A senior can take two kids, but each then learns at three-quarter speed, and she will mention it in the eight-week reports. Slowly the kid may also take on her mentor's character, roughly a one in three chance across a season. The Mentoring tab keeps a record of what each kid has gained. A pairing ends itself when there is nothing left to teach (the kid turns 21, reaches her ceiling or takes on her mentor's character), and one that is not working can be ended on its card.
handbook.a3_f: Yes, at any stoppage. The clipboard button opens tactics and substitutions mid-match, so you can shut a game down, chase one, or get a tiring front row off. Eight women sit on the bench and you can use all eight, which is what the laws allow: front-row cover included. A woman who has come off does not come back, other than the front-row and blood exceptions the referee panel already applies. The game suggests natural cover first rather than putting a winger in the second row.
handbook.a30_f: Three layers. The whole squad has a weekly emphasis; up to five youngsters can carry a development focus for faster growth; and a handful of women can be put on personal plans, individual programmes in a chosen area. Your assistant's badge sets how many plans the department can run at once, the matching specialist coach and the Training Paddock make a plan bite more often, and younger women absorb more of it. A woman on a plan works her programme instead of the squad session, so it is a choice, not a stack. Progress is slow and unglamorous, which is how it should be. Training decides where ability goes, not how much there is: every point a programme adds is paid for by a point from an area it does not cover, taken from what the position needs least, and it stops near what the position plays at. A plan also adds one rating point each summer to anyone below their potential.
handbook.a39_f: A youth intake arrives every season. Your academy coach and the Centre of Excellence both raise the quality of what comes through, and the better your setup the more likely a genuine prospect appears. You get an honest preview before intake day and a graded report afterwards. Development deals run out at 21: promote a girl to a professional contract from her player page before the summer she turns 21, or she leaves as a free agent. You are warned a full season ahead.
handbook.a40_f: Yes, but only when something weakens its hand, and the player page tells you what that is before you bid. The strongest card you can hold is a contract running out in the summer, because they would otherwise lose her for nothing. After that: a woman who has barely played, one who is unhappy, a club sitting in the red, a squad already well stocked in her position, or a player the wrong side of 33. Those stack, up to about a third off in the worst case for the seller. A wanted woman who is playing every week at a solvent club will not move a penny, and the screen says so rather than letting you waste a window finding out.
handbook.a47_f: A player who is performing above her contract will have her camp come knocking. You can meet the demand, haggle a figure of your own, or refuse. Refusing a star has consequences, and so does paying every time.
handbook.a49_f: Yes. On her profile, The Office card lets you praise her form or have a quiet word - two conversations a week across the squad, one per woman. Her personality decides how it lands: a professional answers a warning with work, a mercenary shrugs, and praising a struggling hothead reads as sarcasm. Warning a woman who is playing well insults her, and the dressing room hears about it.
handbook.a5_f: Yes, and Physicality is the dial he decides. Pushing it up buys breakdown power and costs you yellow cards and kickable penalties, and the penalty price scales with the referee in the middle. Measured over eight seasons: in front of a referee who lets a lot go at the tackle, going physical is worth about two and a half points a match to you; in front of one who is fussy there, it costs you about a point and a half. Getting that read right is worth roughly four points a match, which is more than any other single slider is worth on its own. The referee and his interpretations are named on the pre-match briefing before you pick, so the information is always there. Left in the middle the dial costs and buys nothing.
handbook.a71_f: Yes, if one asks. The unions watch managers with a reputation of 64 or better and ring twice a season - the smaller nations first, England, France and New Zealand only for names in the mid-80s. Accept from your Manager Profile and you hold the country alongside the club: the Club & Country screen holds the whole desk - the ranking, the union's confidence, your Test record, and the window squad, which is yours to shape. When camp is open you can drop a name and call the next woman up - any qualified player in the game, no age limit and no rating floor, only the injured refused - the federation caps the room and will not let it fall below 23, and on a Test weekend your assistant minds any club fixture while you take the country. Leave the job and the Test record stays on your Manager Profile for good. Step down from either job from the same screen. A World Championship is the biggest thing in the game. The Job Centre shows how close your reputation is.
handbook.a83_f: The same contest as a ruck, but the ball carrier is still on her feet and players bind on to her. A strong pack drives it forward, which is how a lot of tries are scored from close range.
handbook.a97_f: The front row is two props and a hooker, the women who meet first in a scrum. Add the two locks and it is the tight five, the pushing engine. The back row - two flankers and a number 8 - are the forwards who cover ground.
handbook.a98_f: The scrum-half feeds the ball out of every ruck and scrum, so she touches it more than anyone on the pitch. The fly-half decides what happens next - pass, kick or run - and is usually the goal kicker as well.
handbook.a99_f: The two wings and the full-back: the last line of defence and usually the quickest women in the side. They field kicks, chase them, and finish most of the tries.
handbook.a102_f: A yellow card sends a player to the sin bin for ten minutes and you play a woman short. A red card removes her for the rest of the match. Both cost far more than the penalty that caused them.
handbook.a103_f: A Head Injury Assessment. A player who takes a blow to the head leaves the field to be checked; she returns only if she passes, and the game will not let her back if she does not.

coachfix.attHeadNone: {poss}% of the ball and no tries.
coachfix.attHeadOne: {poss}% of the ball and one try.
coachfix.attHowNarrow: Style is at {n}, which keeps it in the pack. Push it past sixty and the backs will see it.
coachfix.attHowWide: Give the 10 the playmaker role on the Roles tab and drill a different attacking call. Possession without width is just carrying.
coachfix.benchHow: Tap Match-Day Squad at the hour. All {cap} changes are free, but the two or three into the shirts running on empty are the ones that win tight games - past four you are swapping quality out for freshness you do not need.
coachfix.discHowHigh: Physicality is at {n}. Pull it under fifty and the same pack concedes fewer.
coachfix.discHowLow: Drop Physicality a notch and put a leader on culture in the leadership group. Cards are a habit, not luck.
coachfix.discRed: A red card, and down to fourteen for the rest of it.
coachfix.discRedWho: {player} sent off, and down to fourteen for the rest of it.
coachfix.discYcWho: {player} binned: ten minutes a player short.
coachfix.gradeAllDone: Both jobs from last time are done: {fixed}. That is a side that listens.
coachfix.gradeBoth: Last time we asked for two things. {fixed} is sorted. {missed} is not.
coachfix.gradeBothMissed: {missed} were the jobs last time, and neither has moved.
coachfix.gradeOneDone: {fixed} is sorted since last time. Keep doing whatever that was.
coachfix.gradeOneMissed: We asked about {missed} last time, and here it is again.
coachfix.howBreakdown: A jackal flanker on Selection, or push Physicality up. Contested ball is won by bodies arriving, not by shape.
coachfix.howLineout: Get a second genuine jumper into the back five on Selection, and change the lineout call on Set Piece so they stop reading it.
coachfix.howScrum: Pick a heavier front row on Selection, or give a prop the scrummager role on the Roles tab. A dial cannot lift a light tight five.
coachfix.kickOrderHow: Set your first and second kicker on Set Piece. The automatic pick hands the tee to a different player every week.
coachfix.lateHead: They scored {n} of their points after the hour.
coachfix.lateHowFew: You made {changes}. Tap Match-Day Squad at the hour: eight fresh bodies is a weapon you have already paid for.
coachfix.lateHowMany: Drop Tempo so the pack is not running on fumes at sixty, and brief two finishers on the Bench page.
coachfix.lostHead: Beaten without one number screaming about it.
coachfix.lostHow: Run one preset for a fortnight rather than a new plan every Saturday. The engine rewards a side that knows its own game.
coachfix.rolesHeadNone: Not one shirt has a role set.

rolesHeadSome.one: Only {n} shirt has a role set.
rolesHeadSome.other: Only {n} shirts have a role set.

coachfix.rolesHow: Tap a shirt on the Roles tab. A scrummager, a jackal and a playmaker are three small edges you are currently not taking.
coachfix.splitHead: The bench split is on automatic.
coachfix.splitHow: Choose 5-3, 6-2 or 4-4 on the Bench page. Six forwards wins a scrum war, four and four covers an injury anywhere.
coachfix.tankHead: Even after {subs} changes we finished on {mine}% to their {theirs}%.
coachfix.tankHow: Lower Tempo, or set the week to fitness on Prep. This is a conditioning problem rather than a tactical one, and the gym level on Club Infrastructure is the long answer.
coachfix.teeHeadOne: A conversion missed off the tee.
coachfix.teeHow: Name your kicking order on Set Piece rather than leaving it to whoever has the best boot on the pitch. A slump is only yours to answer if you chose the kicker.
coachfix.terrHead: We only had {poss}% of the ball.
coachfix.terrHowElse: Lower Tempo so phases last, and set the exit to counter on Set Piece rather than kicking it to their fullback.
coachfix.terrHowKick: Kicking is at {n}, so we hand it back on purpose. Bring it down and keep the ball in hand.
coachfix.wonHead: Nothing broke, so the work is making it repeatable.
coachfix.wonHow: Leave the Tactics dials alone and pick the same Selection again. The strongest unit was the {unit} - build next week around it.

venue.altHigh: Altitude. The ground sits {alt}m up and the air is thin, so legs go earlier than the clock says. Expect the last quarter to hurt.
venue.altSome: A noticeable climb to {alt}m. Not the highveld, but enough that the forwards will feel the second half.
venue.cold: Cold, and colder than this lot are built for. Keep the ball off the deck and make them handle it.
venue.heat: Heat and humidity nobody in this squad trains in. Hydration and tempo control, or it gets away from us late on.
venue.longHaul: {km}km and {tz} hours of clock change. Long-haul rugby: the squad will not be fresh, whatever the medical room says.
venue.road: {km}km on the road. Not far enough to blame, far enough to notice.
venue.trek: A genuine trek at {km}km. Travel legs are a factor here.
venue.trekTz: A genuine trek at {km}km and {tz} hours of time difference. Travel legs are a factor here.

supporter.refused: The store would not open a purchase for this item. Nothing was charged. Usually this means the product is not on sale in your country, or it is not active yet, or this account is not on the licence-testing list.
supporter.error: The store could not be reached. Nothing was charged - try again later.
supporter.nothingToRestore: Nothing to restore on this account.
supporter.pending: The store is still processing it. Nothing more to do here - it lands on its own, and Restore will pick it up if you close the game first.
supporter.unavailable: There is no store attached to this build, so there is nothing to buy. Nothing is missing from the game.

about.contactBody: A bug, a wrong rating, a name you would rather was not in here - all of it reaches the same person, and the Report a Bug screen attaches the details that make it fixable.
about.communityBody: Report problems in any language, share ideas and talk rugby with other managers on the PHASE Discord.
about.privacyBody: The game collects nothing about you and sends nothing anywhere. Careers are saved on this device only, which is why the Save / Load screen has an Export button - it is the only backup that exists.
about.sub: what this is, and what it takes: nothing
about.thanks: Built for the love of the game. Thank you for playing it.
about.title: About & legal
about.unofficialBody: PHASE: Rugby Manager is not affiliated with, endorsed by or licensed by any player, club, league or governing body. Club names are real; competitions, grounds and sponsors are renamed or invented. Player names are real, used to identify people in a sporting database and for nothing else - and no official badges, kits or logos are included.
about.storeBody: Optional extras - none of it plays the matches.
about.bridgeBody: The store and the adverts come from the app around the game, not from the game itself. If either says not connected, this build of the app was assembled without that piece and nothing in here can switch it on.
about.bridgeProducts: Products priced by the store: {live} of {asked}
